deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematical derivation. It is a printed page (p. XIII) from the historical preface of an 18th-century German arithmetic and algebra textbook. The bundle name 'HB.Leiste' suggests Christian Leiste's 'Die Arithmetik und Algebra', Wolfenbüttel 1790, in a copy that may have been Gauss's. The page continues a survey of the history of algebra and arithmetic.

(1) Vieta's innovations:
- He used capital letters for known quantities.
- He brought equations into convenient form.
- He removed the second term of a mixed ('unreine') quadratic to make it pure, by the 'general formula of §197' (in modern terms x = y - a_{n-1}/(n a_n)).
- He solved the cubic by his own method.
- He treated mixed equations of any degree.
- In 'De emendatione aequationum' he described the nature of equations, on which Harriot and Descartes later built.

(2) The 17th century is praised as the richest period of mathematical discovery, beginning with logarithms in arithmetic:
- Stifel recognised their nature (pairing arithmetic and geometric progressions) but did not apply them to computation.
- Jost Bürgi, mechanic to the Landgrave of Hesse, first did so.
- Kästner obtained Bürgi's 'Arithmetische und geometrische Progreß-Tabuln', Prag 1620, 7½ sheets in quarto, at an auction. The instructions were missing, but Kästner supplied them in his 'Fortsetzung der Rechenkunst', Göttingen 1786, pp. 93 ff.
- Bürgi's logarithms went unnoticed because Napier's appeared first (the text says 1619). Benjamin Ursinus (Behr) of Beuthen, later Joachimsthal Gymnasium in Berlin and professor in Frankfurt (Oder), republished them at once.

Handwritten additions:
- An underline under 'so bald'.
- A correction stroke through the initial letter of 'Unterricht'.
- A marginal correction sign at the right, most plausibly a handwritten Fraktur 'U' after a vertical bar. This is a proofreader-style correction of a damaged or wrong type letter.

No mathematics by the annotator. The only implicit mathematics is the referenced transformation removing the second term of a polynomial. I give it below as a checkable item; this is my own addition.
errors: Historical: Napier's logarithms were first published in 1614 ('Mirifici logarithmorum canonis descriptio'); 1619 is the posthumous 'Constructio'. The text's 1619 is inaccurate.
Historical: removal of the second term was already practised by Cardano (Ars Magna 1545). Attributing it to Vieta as originator is an overstatement, though Vieta systematised it.
Historical: Vieta used capital vowels for unknowns and capital consonants for knowns. The text's 'capital letters for known quantities' is only half the convention.
Historical: Harriot's 'Artis analyticae praxis' appeared posthumously in 1631, after Vieta's 'De emendatione' (1615). The chronology 'Harriot and Descartes later built on it' is broadly fine.
No mathematical errors on the page; there is no mathematics performed.

results.what: Historical survey: Vieta's literal notation, removal of the second term, and Bürgi's and Napier's logarithms (printed textbook preface, not Gauss's work)
results.modern_name: History of algebra/logarithms; Tschirnhaus-type shift x = y - b/(n a) (depressed polynomial)
results.usually_credited_to: Cardano/Vieta (depressing equations); Bürgi (c.1600, printed 1620) and Napier (1614) for logarithms

results.what: Handwritten typographical correction mark (underline 'so bald', corrected letter U in 'Unterricht' with marginal sign)

deep.surprise_reason: Printed historical preface of a textbook (likely Leiste's Arithmetik und Algebra) with only a typographical correction mark; no mathematics by Gauss.

checkable.sympy: a,b,c,y=symbols('a b c y'); expand((a*(y-b/(2*a))**2 + b*(y-b/(2*a)) + c)).coeff(y,1) == 0
checkable.asserts: Substituting x = y - b/(2a) removes the linear (second) term of a quadratic, producing a pure quadratic (Vieta's procedure referenced via §197).

checkable.sympy: a,b,c,d,y=symbols('a b c d y'); simplify(expand(a*(y-b/(3*a))**3 + b*(y-b/(3*a))**2 + c*(y-b/(3*a)) + d).coeff(y,2)) == 0
checkable.asserts: The general formula x = y - b/(n a) removes the second term of a degree-n equation (here n=3).

transcription_corrections: The marginal note '|{+ W [?] +}' is more likely a correction sign: a vertical bar followed by a handwritten Fraktur 'U' (or similar proofreader mark), matching the stroke through the 'U' of 'Unterricht'. It is not a 'W'.
'so bald' is underlined by hand in the original; the transcription does not indicate this.
'{+|+}Unterricht' should be read as a correction stroke on the initial letter of 'Unterricht', not an inserted character.
